verdicts.reason: Explicit praise for the agency is distinct from evidence of a prior working relationship; a first-time commenter can applaud the agency, and a long-standing permit holder can be purely critical.
Both score the same behavior of foregrounding quantified organizational scale (members, employees, market share), so scores would track almost identically.

X requires the persona to be the primary credibility device independent of data or citation, while Y scores the standing claim's specificity regardless of the evidence around it, so an expert comment with tenure plus heavy data scores high on Y and low on X.

X measures substantive precision in mapping the rule to provisions and authority, Y measures legal formatting register, so a plain-prose but provision-precise comment or a law-firm memo of general opposition splits the two.

Y fires on any relational cue including merely naming officials or thanking the agency for coordination, whereas X requires a documented ongoing formal relationship, so a first-time commenter with polite relational language scores high on Y and 0 on X.
Citation of CFR parts is a surface referencing behavior, while an ultra vires statutory-authority argument is a substantive legal claim; either can appear without the other.
Both require self-derived numeric compliance-cost figures with a stated basis, and both zero out when no numbers appear.

X credits any job, ownership, or operational-role positioning, while Y requires tenure or place/trade identity, so a corporate officer describing their operational role with no tenure or locality scores high on X and low on Y.
X covers any procedural or docket-mechanics ask (re-notice, earlier publication, status tracking) on a graded scale, while Y is limited to delay/extension requests as the comment's primary purpose.

X scores disclosure of an internal drafting/consensus process, Y scores claimed breadth of external multi-organization representation; a long coalition sign-on letter with no drafting-process narrative splits them.
Both score the display of institutional scale credentials (size, market share, employees, member lists) to establish authority, and the extra items in X co-occur with those scale claims.

Y imposes a proportion threshold, explicitly scoring 0 for a brief one-line self-identification, whereas X scores 10 for any explicit itemization of size, so a single sentence of employee and market-share figures splits the two.
Both detect mass-campaign form-letter text from within the document (formulaic, duplicated, non-individualized wording) and both zero out on bespoke prose.

Y requires expert credentials such as senior title, licensing, or specialized expertise, while X also credits plain local identity and hands-on operational roles, so a lifelong fisherman or resident scores high on X and low on Y.

X gates on density and length (multiple lengthy unpersonalized paragraphs), whereas Y fires on formulaic slogans regardless of length, so a short three-sentence form letter scores high on Y and low on X.
Both name professional regulatory-legal competence in rulemaking (procedural terminology, provision-level engagement, structured edits) and would rank comments almost identically.
Both score explicit disclosure of prior dealings with the issuing agency (permits, recurring meetings, prior communications) and both zero out for an unaffiliated first-time commenter.

X requires case-law citations or a counsel signature block, while Y also fires on rigid memo structure and dense legalese alone, so a structured trade-association memo with no case citations splits the two.
X requires described prior dealings, whereas Y also credits merely naming officials or thanking the agency for coordination, which a first-time commenter can do.
Generic campaign boilerplate and dense accumulation of statutes, cases, and studies are opposite registers and routinely appear in different comments.
Both score the same artifact set left by the submission pipeline (email/portal headers, attachment placeholders, filenames, OCR errors, duplicated cover text).
The scales run in opposite directions, and X's 0 pole also covers dense technical or scientific prose with no legalese at all, which Y would score 0.
Both score whether a concrete, implementable alternative regulatory design is offered, and both zero out when the comment only objects.
Both score claimed breadth of multi-organization or membership representation and consensus, keyed on the same cues of long member lists and named signatories.

Authority stacking is undisciplined citation volume including studies and executive orders, while regulatory-lawyer fluency is precise provision-level engagement; a tight redline of one CFR section is high on Y and low on X.
First-hand operational description and emotional intensity are independent; a calm operator account or an outraged uninvolved citizen splits them.
Both score advertisement of institutional scale credentials (size, membership, market share, reach), and their trigger lists overlap almost entirely.

X credits substantive procedural precision and structured proposed edits even in plain prose, while Y keys on legal memo formatting and legalese, so a precise but plainly written comment scores high on X and 0 on Y.
